rationale: B wins because it finds one more real lane: “Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost, including Airtable” turns unfinished pricing into a usable SaaS business-model story. A’s sharpest line, “won't say how often they get it right,” has teeth, but it slides from “not disclosed” into a refusal Airtable has not actually made. B is less cleanly grounded, but it is more useful to a founder because it separates pitch-ready repositioning from proof-dependent risk stories.
gaps_in_A: “won't say how often they get it right” overstates the supplied fact; “agent-reliability data not disclosed” is not the same as an on-record refusal.
“in a category that already has incumbents” needs an actual competitor contrast; the set admits this later, but the headline spends proof it does not yet have.
“Draft one tight pitch around it” points the founder toward the most adversarial, proof-poor angle before getting reliability or safeguard answers.
A treats unfinalized pricing only as a weakness and misses a distinct pricing/business-model angle hiding in the fact block.
gaps_in_B: “Airtable, Notion, Smartsheet and Monday” adds named competitor context not supplied in the update; useful, but unverified in this blind brief.
“Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost” overgeneralizes from Airtable’s unfinalized pricing. One company’s open pricing is not proof of a market-wide problem.
“established category leader” is an extra status claim. The update says Airtable serves many enterprise teams, not that it leads the category.
“many teams treat as an operational source of truth” is plausible enterprise framing, but stronger than the supplied fact and needs confirmation.
